deckName: KS3 DT · J3 Lesson 1 — The Studio Opens (Teacher Deck)

slides.kicker: OUR LADY'S GRAMMAR SCHOOL · DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY
slides.heading: Lesson 1 · The Studio Opens
slides.sub: Your first Digital Technology lesson of the year — J3 · Lesson 1 of 17
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: seated, logged in to the computer, nothing else open. These pupils have never used this website before, and this is their first-ever sign-in to it.

SAY: "Good morning. Books away, hands off the mice, and look up here — this hour starts with me, not with the computers."

WHY: this is their last year of Digital Technology before GCSE and the hour is built to say so, so open it like something that matters.

WHEN TO MOVE: as soon as the room is settled.

slides.heading: In this lesson you will…
bullets: Find out what your Studio year builds: you make real work, you learn to judge it, and you get better at choosing.
Find your way around this website, and see where your work is saved.
Go back over the studio code — the six DT room rules you already know — and take on a new job with it.
Show where you are starting from in Portfolio Zero, which is not a test and cannot be failed.
Find your Compass: what kind of work you actually enjoy.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: still eyes front, screens ignored.

SAY: "Five things today." Then read the five lines out.

WATCH FOR: the fourth line is the one to land hardest. A class that believes Portfolio Zero counts will guess badly, and the whole value of it is that it is honest.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: What The Studio means
bullets: Your Digital Technology year is called The Studio, because you work the way a real studio works.
You CREATE real work: programs you write yourself, data you turn into something worth reading, and web pages you design for somebody else to use.
You learn to JUDGE work, your own and other people's, against a standard instead of a feeling.
And you get better at CHOOSING, because by the end you have real evidence about what you are good at.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: eyes front.

SAY: "Three words for the whole year: create, judge, choose." Then read the four lines out.

WHY: every lesson this year lands under one of those three words, and the pupils' own opening card says the same thing in the same words a few minutes from now.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: Why this year is worth doing
bullets: In JANUARY you pick your GCSE options. Digital Technology is one of the subjects on that list, and it is optional.
Plenty of people will pick it and plenty will not, and both of those are fine answers.
If you do pick it there are two routes inside it, Multimedia and Programming, and by January you will know far more about which kind of work you enjoy.
If you do not pick it, everything this year teaches you is still yours.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: eyes front. This is the slide the room will have questions about, so take it slowly.

SAY: read all four lines exactly as they stand. They are the facts and they are load-bearing: the options window is JANUARY, not the end of the year, and Digital Technology is an optional subject.

IF A PUPIL ASKS WHETHER THEY HAVE TO PICK DT: "No. It is one of the choices, not a requirement." Say it plainly — it is on the slide because it is true.

DO NOT SAY: anything that suggests a pupil has been sorted into a route, or that this hour decides anything. No pupil should leave thinking either.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: Ready? Go.
bullets: Open Google Classroom, then click the Digital Technology Lesson 1 link.
Read the opening card together — it types itself out, so wait for the last line.
Then work on your own. The screen gives you five short steps, one at a time.
When a card pops up to say you have finished that part, stop and look up. That card is your badge.
Stuck on the way? Click the round ? button at the bottom right, then put your hand up.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to open the website for the first time.

SAY: "Google Classroom first, then the Digital Technology Lesson 1 link. Nothing else." Wait until the room is on the opening card before you say another word.

THEN SAY: "We are going to read this together." The card types itself out, so wait for the last line, then read it aloud while pupils follow on their own screens. It repeats the options facts in the pupils' own words and explains what those Google permission screens were for.

THEN SAY: "Work through the five steps on your own. When your badge card pops up, stop and look up."

WATCH FOR: if the link is not on Google Classroom, put the QR code from the Classes tab on the board instead. And walk the room — the pupils who need you are the ones who cannot find something on screen.

WHEN TO MOVE: when the first badge cards appear, stop the whole room for the studio code.

slides.heading: Five things to find
bullets: The Year map button at the top left. It takes you back to the page with all seventeen lessons on it — but do not press it yet.
The padlocks on your year map. Nearly every tile has one, and that is normal: each lesson opens on the day the class does it.
The small green word Saved at the top right. There is no save button on this website.
The round ? button at the bottom right. It gives you help for the screen you are on.
Your own name at the top right. It opens your Wardrobe, which holds the different looks your screen can wear.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: on the second screen of the lesson, working down five short steps.

SAY: "Seven minutes on this now saves you a term of putting your hand up. Each step tells you exactly what to look for."

THEN SAY, pointing at the picture: "The steps come one at a time. You tick the box yourself once you have found the thing, and the next step then appears. There is nothing to hurry."

WATCH FOR: the padlock step. A locked tile looks like a fault to a pupil who has never seen this website, and every tile except today's is locked. Say that one out loud yourself rather than leaving it to the screen.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the badge slide while they work.

slides.heading: Badges, points and your Wardrobe
bullets: There are four big parts to this lesson. Finish one and the website gives you a badge — a picture in your own record that says you did it.
Every badge brings points. On the badge card the points are called XP.
Points unlock new looks for your screen, and your looks are kept in your Wardrobe.
Once you have unlocked a look it stays yours for the rest of the year.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: finishing the five steps. The first badge card is appearing on screens around the room.

SAY: "That card is a badge. There are four of them in this hour. Nothing is handed out and nothing is printed — a badge is a picture in your own record on this website, and it comes with points."

WATCH FOR: a pupil who opens the Wardrobe and asks whether that is all there is. On day one it holds three looks — the one that pupil's screen is wearing and the two this lesson can unlock — and the rest arrive as the year unlocks new levels. That pupil is reading it right: it is the beginning of a collection, not the whole of it.

WHEN TO MOVE: when badge cards have appeared around the room, stop everybody.

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The Studio Code
bullets: A working studio writes its rules down, and then somebody has to decide whether people are keeping them.
Today that somebody is you. You read six real situations and judge each one.
For each one you decide whether it is IN LINE with the code or AGAINST it.
Watch out: not every case is somebody doing something wrong.
Nothing wrong here is a real answer, and it is the right answer more than once.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: first badge earned, screens ignored, eyes front.

SAY: "These are the same six DT room rules you already know — there is nothing new in them. What is new is the job. A working studio writes its rules down as a code of conduct, and then somebody has to decide whether people are keeping it. Today that somebody is you."

THEN SAY, and it is the sentence that changes how the class works: "Not every case is somebody doing something wrong. Nothing wrong here is a real answer, and it is the right answer more than once."

WHY: without that line pupils hunt for a fault in every case and get the clean ones wrong for the wrong reason.

DO NOT SAY: how many of the six are clean. The lesson tells them only that it happens more than once, and that is deliberate.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the next slide, then send them in.

slides.heading: What a case looks like
bullets: A card explains the job, then the first case opens.
You read what happened, then click the answer that matches it.
Every case is marked the moment you click, and you are told why.
After the six there are two harder cases. They are optional — do them if you want, or press Stop here instead.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to press into the first case.

SAY: "The picture on the right is the card that opens it. The cases then come one at a time."

THEN SAY: "The two hard cases at the end are optional. There is a Stop here instead button beside them and nothing is taken off you for pressing it."

WHY: pupils only take an optional challenge if they believe it is optional, so say it rather than leaving it on the screen.

WHILE THEY WORK: circulate, and read the reasons over shoulders rather than the marks. The interesting pupil is the one who picked a defensible wrong answer, and the reason on screen tells you which rule that pupil was weighing.

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the class has judged the sixth case, stop the room. Pupils still on the two hard cases can finish them.

slides.heading: STOP — Portfolio Zero
bullets: A portfolio is the collection of work somebody shows to prove what they can do.
This is yours before you have made any of it — the zero at the start.
Twelve quick questions. It is NOT a test, you cannot fail it, and nobody is marking it.
Nine of them you might work out. Three just ask how you feel about your own work.
You will not be told right or wrong, and that is on purpose.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: the studio code judged, facing front.

SAY, and set the tone in one go before anybody starts it: "A portfolio is the collection of work somebody shows to prove what they can do, and this is yours before you have made any of it. Quiet and on your own now. Twelve quick questions. It is not a test, you cannot fail it, and I am not marking it. Most of the nine are about things nobody has taught you yet, so not knowing is completely normal. The last three have no right answer at all — they just ask how you feel about your own work, so say what is true."

WHY: the thing that ruins a starting-point record is a pupil who thinks it counts, so it is worth saying twice. Say the word portfolio out loud as well: the year is built on it and most of the class will not have met it.

IF A PUPIL ASKS WHETHER IT GIVES YOU A SCORE: nothing is marked on a pupil's screen and no pupil is ever told right or wrong. On the staff side you get a picture of how the class answered the nine, and that is for your planning. That is the honest answer and it is the one to give.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the next slide, then let them start.

slides.heading: What Portfolio Zero looks like
bullets: One question at a time, with four answers to choose from.
When you click, the screen says Answer saved and nothing else. That is it working.
There is no right-or-wrong message on these, so there is nothing to compare with anybody.
You read this back twice: before your options in January, and again in the last lesson of the year.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to start twelve questions on their own, in silence.

SAY: "The screen will say Answer saved and nothing else. That is it working, not the website being broken."

WHY: somebody always asks, and answering it once to the whole room saves answering it at desk after desk.

WATCH FOR: the picture on the right is what they will see twelve times over — a question and four answers. The words Answer saved appear where the chosen answer was, a moment after a pupil clicks, and that is the whole of the response.

WHILE THEY WORK: this is the quietest part of the hour and the best chance to catch up with anyone whose sign-in was awkward at the start.

WHEN TO MOVE: when the room has finished.

slides.heading: STOP — Your Compass
bullets: Portfolio Zero asked what you can DO. Your Compass asks what you ENJOY.
Three questions, each with two things to choose between.
Neither side is better than the other and there is no right answer.
Pick the one that sounds more like you, even if it is only slightly more.
Your Compass decides nothing. It is where you are standing today.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: Portfolio Zero finished, facing front. This is the last new thing in the hour.

SAY: "Portfolio Zero asked what you can do. This asks something completely different: what you actually enjoy. Three questions, two things to choose between each time, and neither side is better than the other. Pick the one that sounds more like you, even if it is only slightly more."

THEN SAY, because it is the sentence that stops a pupil worrying: "Your Compass decides nothing at all. It is where you are standing today, and today is the first day of the year. You look at it again in January, and people do change their minds."

WHAT THE RESULT DOES: it names the kind of digital work the pupil most ENJOYS first, and only then mentions which GCSE route that side of the work belongs to. That order is the point — a pupil who never takes the subject still gets a true answer about what they enjoy. Landing near the middle is a real result, not a failure to decide, and on the first day of a year it will be the commonest one.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: What the Compass looks like
bullets: Three pairs on one screen. You can change any of them until you press the button.
Then a needle settles, and you are told in plain words what it found.
If you pick all three on one side, it lands firmly there. If you split them, it settles near the middle.
Near the middle is a real answer, and on the first day of a year it is the most common one.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to answer the three pairs.

SAY: "All three pairs are on one screen, and you can change your mind until you press the button at the bottom. The button stays locked until you have picked one from each pair, and the screen says so."

WATCH FOR: read the result with them if the room is quiet enough. It gives the kind of work the pupil ENJOYS first — designing and communicating, or building and problem-solving — and the GCSE route mapping second.

WHEN TO MOVE: when the needles have settled and the badge cards have landed.

slides.heading: Where this year goes
bullets: One card before you finish, with a picture of GCSE Digital Technology on it.
Everybody who takes it does the same core work first. Then it splits into two routes: Multimedia, and Programming.
You do not choose anything today. That choice belongs to your options in January, and the subject is optional.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: Compass settled, reading one card on their own.

SAY: "One card about where the year goes, with a picture of the two routes on it. Nobody chooses anything today."

WHY: the card is a diagram, not a decision, and it says so in its own words. This is the one place in the hour where the two route names are worth reading out, because the pupils' own screens name them and so does the last question.

WHEN TO MOVE: as soon as the card is confirmed. TAKE THIS SLIDE DOWN before the last two screens — see the next slide for why.

slides.heading: The last two screens
bullets: One question, on your own. This one IS marked, so think about it.
You find out how you did right at the end, after the last screen.
Then How did it go?, where you say honestly how the hour went.
The comment box goes to your teacher and nobody else. Everyone finishes this screen before leaving.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: working through the last two screens on their own.

PUT THIS SLIDE UP AND TAKE THE ROUTES SLIDE DOWN. The marked question is about the two routes, so leaving the routes slide on the wall would hand the class the answer while they answer it.

SAY: "One question now, on your own, and this one is marked — so think about it. You find out how you did right at the end, after the last screen, so do not sit waiting for an answer."

THEN SAY: "Then tell me honestly how today went. The comment box comes to me and nobody else."

WATCH FOR: the picture on the right is the final screen — three sentences to rate, a how-it-felt choice and a comment box.

NOBODY LEAVES WITHOUT FINISHING How did it go? It is compulsory, and it is how you hear from the pupils who never put a hand up. In this hour it matters more than usual: a pupil who is anxious about options will often say it here and nowhere else.

WHEN TO MOVE: when both screens are done.

slides.heading: Before you leave
bullets: Sign out every time. If you stay signed in, anything the next person does on this computer looks like you did it.
Chair in, area tidy, nothing left beside your machine.
Next time: First Words in Python. You write real code in it, starting from your very first line.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: finished, packing up.

SAY: "Two jobs before you stand up. Sign out — if you stay signed in, anything the next person does on this computer looks like you did it. Then chair in, area tidy, nothing left beside your machine."

WHY: the class has just spent the biggest part of the hour judging other people for exactly these two things, so this is the moment they land.

WHEN TO MOVE: dismiss when the room is signed out and tidy.
